extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether patent claims recite patent-eligible subject matter under the Alice/Mayo framework (Step 2A/2B), including factors for transformations, well‑understood/routine/conventional activity, meaningful limitations, and mere instructions to apply an exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particularity or generality of the transformation
rubrics_metrics.description: When a transformation is recited in a claim, evaluate the particularity or generality of the transformation; more particular transformations (e.g., tanning, dyeing, vulcanizing) are more likely to provide 'significantly more' and confine the patent monopoly within definite bounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme Court examples (Gottschalk v. Benson / Corning v. Burden) show transformations that change an article/material in a sufficiently definite way are stronger. More particular transformations likely provide significantly more than the judicial exception; generic or vague transformations less so. Example: Tilghman (fat into fatty acids/glycerine) and Diamond v. Diehr (rubber molding) are favorable examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particularity of the recited article
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the degree to which the recited article being transformed is particular versus generically recited; transformations applied to specifically-identified articles are more likely to provide significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A transformation applied to a generically recited article or 'any and all articles' likely does not provide significantly more than the judicial exception. A transformation that can be specifically identified or limited to particular articles is more likely to integrate the judicial exception into a practical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature and extent of the transformation (change in state or thing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the type/extent of the change produced by the transformation; transformations that change function or use are more likely to provide significantly more than those that only change location or superficial attributes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transformations resulting in a different function/use (e.g., raw synthetic rubber into precision-molded products — Diehr) are likely to provide significantly more. Mere relocation or insignificant change is less likely to do so.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of the article transformed (physical vs intangible)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the transformation affects a physical/tangible object/substance versus an intangible concept; transformations of physical/tangible things are more likely to integrate a judicial exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transformation of physical/tangible objects/substances favors eligibility; transformation of intangibles (contractual obligations, mental judgments) is less likely to provide significantly more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the transformation is extra-solution activity or a field-of-use limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the transformation meaningfully limits execution of the claimed method steps or is merely extra‑solution activity/field‑of‑use (nominal contribution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A transformation that contributes only nominally or insignificantly to claim execution (e.g., mere data‑gathering or field‑of‑use limitation) will not provide significantly more. Example: Mayo — administering a drug was found by the Supreme Court to be only a field-of-use limitation and not significantly more. See MPEP §2106.05(g) & (h) for more on insignificant extra-solution activity and field of use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-understood, routine, conventional activity (general consideration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether additional element(s) are well-understood, routine, conventional activities previously known in the industry; this consideration is evaluated in Step 2B of the eligibility analysis and, if present at a high level, does not favor eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the additional element is a specific limitation that is unconventional/non-routine and confines the claim to a particular useful application, it favors eligibility. If the additional element is no more than well-known, routine, conventional activity recited at a high level, it generally does not amount to significantly more. Examples: DDR Holdings (additional elements favored eligibility because they modified conventional Internet protocol behavior); Mayo (measuring metabolite levels was routine and thus not inventive).

rubrics_metrics.name: Factual determination and forms of support for conventionality
rubrics_metrics.description: A factual determination is required to support a conclusion that additional element(s) are well-understood, routine, conventional activity; examiners may rely on what courts or those in the art recognize as conventional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior art search is not always necessary; examiners should rely on specification statements, court decisions, publications, or take official notice. The examiner must be able to readily conclude, based on expertise or disclosed support, that the element is widely prevalent or in common use. Appropriate supports: (a) specification/applicant statements, (b) court decisions, (c) publications, (d) official notice. The factual determination must be expressly supported in writing (see MPEP §2106.07(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination of conventional elements may still be inventive
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if individual additional elements are well‑understood/routine/conventional, their particular combination may amount to an inventive concept that provides significantly more than the judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A new combination of known steps can be patentable (Diamond v. Diehr). Examples: Rapid Litigation Mgmt. (repeating freeze/thaw steps contrary to art was non-routine), BASCOM (generic network components in a non-conventional arrangement provided technical improvement). Examiners should evaluate elements individually and in combination and explain why combinations do or do not amount to significantly more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer functions recognized as well-understood/routine/conventional (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have recognized certain generic computer functions as well-understood, routine, conventional when recited at a high level or as insignificant extra-solution activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed examples include: (i) receiving or transmitting data over a network (using Internet to gather data); (ii) performing repetitive calculations; (iii) electronic recordkeeping (creating/maintaining logs/accounts); (iv) storing and retrieving information in memory; (v) electronically scanning or extracting data (OCR); (vi) web browser back/forward functionality. Note: DDR Holdings shows that specifying how Internet interactions are manipulated can overcome this presumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Life-science/laboratory techniques recognized as well-understood/routine/conventional (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have recognized certain lab techniques as well‑understood, routine, conventional when claimed generically or as insignificant extra‑solution activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: (i) determining biomarker levels in blood by any means; (ii) using PCR to amplify/detect DNA; (iii) detecting DNA or enzymes in a sample; (iv) immunizing a patient; (v) analyzing DNA sequence or allelic variants; (vi) freezing and thawing cells; (vii) amplifying and sequencing nucleic acids; (viii) hybridizing a gene probe. Generic recitation of these techniques may not add significantly more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other activities courts have found routine/conventional (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Other non-technical activities have been recognized by courts as well-understood, routine, conventional when claimed at a high level or as insignificant extra-solution activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: recording a customer's order; shuffling/dealing a standard deck of cards; restricting public access by requiring viewing an advertisement; presenting offers and gathering statistics; determining estimated outcomes and setting price; arranging hierarchies, sorting information, eliminating less restrictive pricing info and determining price. These generic activities alone typically do not render a claim significantly more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other meaningful limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the claim includes other meaningful limitations beyond generally linking the judicial exception to a particular technological environment; meaningful limitations can transform a judicial exception into patent-eligible subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Considerations in MPEP §2106.05(a)-(d) are meaningful limitations when they amount to significantly more or integrate an exception into a practical application. Example: Diamond v. Diehr (steps like installing rubber, measuring temperature, automatically opening press limited use of a math equation and were meaningful). Classen: immunization step integrated analysis into specific, tangible method. Contrasting examples: Alice (data processing system merely linked the idea to computers) and OIP (testing/collecting data were conventional data-gathering and not meaningful). Evaluate elements individually and as a combination and explain on the record why additional elements meaningfully limit the exception when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere instructions to apply an exception (the 'apply it' rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether additional elements amount to nothing more than reciting the judicial exception plus words to 'apply it' (mere instructions to implement an abstract idea on a generic computer), which does not render the claim eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme Court: a claim must do 'more than simply state the [judicial exception] while adding the words ‘apply it’' (Alice, Mayo). Examples where courts found mere instructions: Mayo (measuring metabolite levels was mere instruction to apply law of nature), Alice (recitation of a computer was mere instruction). This does not require narrowness for eligibility (some broad claims are eligible), so examiners should evaluate all other considerations (improvement, particular machine, transformation, well-understood routine conventional) to determine if a claim is more than mere instructions. If limitations are mere instructions, examiner should explain why they do not meaningfully limit the claim in the rejection (see MPEP §2106.07(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard for making a Step 2B rejection based on conventionality
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection under Step 2B should only be made if the examiner, relying on expertise, can conclude that the additional elements do not amount to significantly more (i.e., are only well-understood, routine, conventional).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If elements/functions are beyond those recognized in the art or by the courts as well-understood, routine, conventional, they will in most cases favor eligibility. Examiners must provide express support for factual determinations and may rely on specification statements, court precedent, publications, or official notice. See MPEP §2106.07(a) for guidance on formulating eligibility rejections and required written support.
